title: The Awakening
author: Kate Chopin
setting: Grand Isle and Chênière Caminada on the Louisiana coast, and the Creole quarter of New Orleans
lengthNote: Thirty-nine chapters, several of them under two pages
openingLine: A green and yellow parrot, which hung in a cage outside the door, kept repeating over and over: “Allez vous-en! Allez vous-en! Sapristi! That’s all right!”
summary: A New Orleans broker's wife spends a summer at a Gulf resort, learns to swim at twenty-eight, and comes back to the city unwilling to keep her Tuesdays at home. Chopin tracks what follows with almost no editorial comment: the painting, the money, the smaller house, the two men, the friend who tells her to think of the children. The novel was reviewed as immoral, went quietly out of print, and was read properly seventy years later.

sourceText.label: Standard Ebooks text of The Awakening
sourceText.note: Chapters are numbered I to XXXIX, following the 1899 first edition; references below give the chapter only.

atAGlance.label: Completed
atAGlance.note: Chopin dated the finished manuscript; it had been begun the previous year under the title A Solitary Soul.

atAGlance.label: First published
atAGlance.note: By Herbert S. Stone & Company of Chicago, in an edition that sold modestly and was not reprinted in her lifetime.

atAGlance.label: Setting
atAGlance.note: Real places, a summer apart: a Creole resort on the Gulf and a household in the city that runs on visiting days and other people's labour.

atAGlance.label: Shape
atAGlance.note: Very short units, many of them a single scene, with the largest decisions taking place in the gaps between them.

structure.label: Chapters I–XIII
structure.title: A summer at the shore
structure.summary: Léonce Pontellier looks up from his newspaper at a sunburnt wife and sees damaged property. Over the weeks that follow Edna sits with Adèle Ratignolle, hears Mademoiselle Reisz play, and finally swims out alone at night further than she has strength to return. The next morning she and Robert Lebrun cross to Chênière Caminada and she sleeps through most of a day.

scenes.title: The gallery
scenes.summary: The parrot, the husband's newspaper, the Creole frankness Edna cannot match, and Robert attached to her for the season.

scenes.title: Two kinds of music
scenes.summary: Adèle's playing keeps company; Mademoiselle Reisz's undoes Edna entirely in a room full of people.

scenes.title: The swim
scenes.summary: Edna swims out alone, refuses to be walked home, and crosses to the Chênière the following morning with Robert.

structure.label: Chapters XIV–XVIII
structure.title: Robert goes to Mexico, and the season ends
structure.summary: Robert announces at a few hours' notice that he is leaving for Mexico, and Edna discovers how much has been arranged without reference to her. Back in New Orleans she abandons her reception day, throws her wedding ring on the carpet, and finds that her husband's response is to consult a doctor about her health.

scenes.title: The announcement
scenes.summary: Robert's departure; Edna tells Adèle that she would give her life for her children but not herself.

scenes.title: The city
scenes.summary: The abandoned Tuesday, the ring on the carpet, and a visit to the Ratignolles that leaves her flat.

structure.label: Chapters XIX–XXVIII
structure.title: Painting, money, and two visitors
structure.summary: Edna paints in the atelier, goes to the races, lets Alcée Arobin into the house, and begins to keep accounts of her own. Mademoiselle Reisz reads her Robert's letters and tells her what it takes to be an artist; her father visits, her husband goes to New York, and the children are sent to their grandmother.

scenes.title: Doing as she likes
scenes.summary: The atelier, the abandoned household routine, and Doctor Mandelet's cautious diagnosis.

scenes.title: The races and the letters
scenes.summary: Arobin's attentions, Reisz's test of her shoulder blades, and the decision to take a small house of her own.

scenes.title: After
scenes.summary: A night with Arobin, and a morning of understanding rather than shame.

structure.label: Chapters XXIX–XXXIV
structure.title: The dinner, and the small house
structure.summary: Edna gives a farewell dinner at her husband's table, wearing a crown of jewels and looking, to one guest, like a woman entirely alone. She moves into the little house around the corner, paid for out of her own winnings and her sketches, and Robert walks back into the city and into Mademoiselle Reisz's rooms.

scenes.title: The birthday dinner
scenes.summary: Nine guests, too much wine, and a hostess presiding over the end of a household.

scenes.title: The pigeon house
scenes.summary: A house small enough to be hers, and Robert's return, awkward and formal, at her own table.

structure.label: Chapters XXXV–XXXIX
structure.title: Adèle's confinement, and the water again
structure.summary: Robert says at last what he has been imagining — that he had hoped Léonce might set her free — and Edna tells him she is not anyone's to give away. She is called out to Adèle's childbirth, hears the words about the children, walks home, finds Robert gone, and goes back to Grand Isle in the morning.

scenes.title: The little café
scenes.summary: Robert's plan for her freedom and Edna's refusal of the terms it assumes.

scenes.title: The birth
scenes.summary: Adèle's confinement, witnessed against Edna's will, and a whispered instruction.

scenes.title: Grand Isle
scenes.summary: A last conversation with Doctor Mandelet, an empty house, and the beach out of season.

characters.name: Edna Pontellier
characters.role: A Kentucky-born woman of twenty-eight, married to a New Orleans broker
characters.summary: She married partly by accident and partly because her father disapproved, and she has been performing a role ever since without noticing that it was one. What the novel gives her is not a plan but a sequence of refusals, and Chopin is careful that she never finds a vocabulary adequate to what she wants.
characters.clue: She learned to swim at twenty-eight, stopped receiving visitors on Tuesdays, moved into a house she could pay for herself, and told a man who offered to ask her husband to release her that she was not his to give.
traits: without a model for what she wants

characters.name: Léonce Pontellier
characters.role: A New Orleans broker, Edna's husband
characters.summary: He is not cruel, and that is the difficulty: he sends bonbons from New York, pays every bill, and genuinely cannot understand why a wife would object to being valued. When Edna becomes unmanageable he consults a doctor, and when she moves out he puts a notice in the paper about redecorating so that nobody's credit suffers.
characters.clue: He looked at his sunburnt wife the way a man looks at a piece of damaged property, and when she left his house he told the newspapers he was having it renovated.

characters.name: Robert Lebrun
characters.role: The son of the Grand Isle proprietor
characters.summary: He has spent every summer attaching himself harmlessly to a married woman, and is caught out when one of them takes it seriously. His final proposal — that Léonce might be persuaded to set her free — shows that he has understood nothing, and he leaves rather than face what she has actually said.
characters.clue: He made a summer profession of devotion to married women, went to Mexico when it stopped being a game, and came back with a plan that still required another man's permission.

characters.name: Adèle Ratignolle
characters.role: Edna's friend at Grand Isle, a Creole mother
characters.summary: She is the novel's mother-woman and is not caricatured: she is warm, shrewd, physically frank, and the person who first gets Edna talking about herself. She also delivers the sentence that does most damage, at the moment when Edna is least able to argue with it.
characters.clue: She embodies everything Edna is expected to be, gave the novel its one scene of childbirth, and whispered four words about the children that follow Edna to the beach.
traits: entirely within the world she was given

characters.name: Mademoiselle Reisz
characters.role: A pianist, disliked by nearly everyone
characters.summary: She is unmarried, ill-tempered, badly dressed and the best musician in the book, and she is the only character who tells Edna the truth about what an independent life would cost. Her test — feeling the shoulder blades for wings — is affectionate and entirely serious.
characters.clue: She played Chopin in a room full of holidaymakers and left one listener in tears, kept a stove, a piano and a window over the river, and asked to feel a friend's shoulder blades for wings.

characters.name: Alcée Arobin
characters.summary: He is practised, unserious and entirely unembarrassed, and the novel declines to punish either of them for what happens between them. What Edna feels afterwards is neither shame nor love but a kind of clarity, and Chopin's refusal to moralise that scene is one of the reasons the book was condemned in 1899.
characters.clue: He showed a married woman the scar from an old duel to get her attention, and was the one man in the book who wanted nothing from her but the present evening.

characters.name: Doctor Mandelet
characters.summary: Called in to explain a wife to a husband, he declines to pathologise her and watches instead. He is the one man who guesses what is happening, and his offer to listen comes on the night Edna has already decided there is nothing left to say.
characters.clue: Asked to treat a woman's disobedience as an illness, he advised letting her alone, and later told her that youth and illusions are the trap nature sets for mothers.

characters.name: Victor Lebrun
characters.role: Robert's younger brother, left in charge at Grand Isle
characters.summary: He is careless, boastful and useful to the structure: he supplies gossip about Robert, sings the song Edna cannot get out of her head, and is the last person to speak to her. He is hammering at a shutter out of season when she walks down to the water.
characters.clue: He sang a line of a song that followed a woman all winter, and was mending a house out of season on the last morning of the book.

themes.name: Waking, and what it costs
themes.summary: Chopin's title names a process rather than an event, and the process is mostly subtraction: Edna stops receiving visitors, stops attending weddings, stops pretending to be interested. The novel is careful that waking supplies no programme — the light that dawns in Chapter VI is described as the kind that shows the way and forbids it.
themes.development: The vague anguish of Chapter III, the formulation in Chapter VI, the swim in Chapter X, the plain statement in Chapter XIX that she began to do as she liked, and the conversation with Doctor Mandelet about being a dupe to illusions.

themes.name: Marriage as a market
themes.summary: Léonce's affection is expressed as inventory: he checks her for damage, sends expensive parcels, and is complimented by the town on his generosity. Edna's rebellion takes the same vocabulary and turns it around, until she can say flatly that she is not among her husband's possessions and will give herself where she chooses.
themes.development: The opening inspection of Chapter I, the wedding ring stamped on in Chapter XVII, the accounts and winnings of the middle chapters, and the refusal offered to Robert in Chapter XXXVI.

themes.name: Mothers and children
themes.summary: The novel sets a woman who is entirely absorbed in her children beside one who loves hers and will not be dissolved by them, and declines to call either of them a bad mother. Edna's formula — she would give her money and her life but not herself — is tested by the one thing the book will not let her avoid, which is Adèle's confinement.
themes.development: The mother-women of Chapter IV, the distinction drawn for Adèle in Chapter XVI, the whispered instruction in Chapter XXXVII, and the thought of Raoul and Etienne in the last pages.

themes.name: Art as a vocation
themes.summary: Edna paints, sells sketches and pays for a house with the proceeds, which makes the question of whether she is an artist a financial one as well as a spiritual one. Mademoiselle Reisz supplies the standard — a courageous soul that dares and defies — and it is a standard the novel does not simply hand to Edna.
themes.development: The atelier in Chapter XIX, Reisz's test of the shoulder blades in Chapter XXVII, the money that buys the pigeon house, and Reisz's imagined sneer in Chapter XXXIX.

themes.name: Isolation
themes.summary: The original title was A Solitary Soul, and the book keeps discovering that Edna's independence and her loneliness are the same fact. Every person she might have confided in — a husband, a lover, a friend, a doctor, a pianist — is available on terms that would require her to become somebody else.
themes.development: The 'abysses of solitude' of Chapter VI, the depression after the Ratignolles' domestic evening, the empty pigeon house after Robert goes, and the entirely deserted beach of the last chapter.

themes.name: The sea as voice and limit
themes.summary: The Gulf is where Edna first does something no one has done for her, and the passage describing its voice is printed twice, thirty-three chapters apart, with almost no alteration. Chopin makes the water both the medium of her freedom and the thing she has no strength to come back from.
themes.development: The first statement of the sea passage in Chapter VI, the night swim in Chapter X, and the same words returning at the opening of Chapter XXXIX.

techniques.name: Free indirect style
techniques.definition: Third-person narration that takes on the vocabulary and bias of the character it follows.
techniques.inThisBook: The narration stays inside Edna's perception while declining to explain her, so that phrases like 'she began to do as she liked' arrive with the flatness of her own thinking rather than the emphasis a moralising narrator would supply.

techniques.name: The repeated sentence
techniques.definition: A passage reprinted almost word for word at a distance, so that the second appearance carries the first with it.
techniques.inThisBook: The description of the sea's voice appears in Chapter VI, near the beginning of Edna's awakening, and again at the start of Chapter XXXIX with the tenses and the setting unchanged — the reader recognises it before Edna reaches the water.

techniques.name: Symbolic objects
techniques.definition: An object the narrative keeps returning to until it stands for the argument rather than illustrating it.
techniques.inThisBook: A parrot in a cage speaking a language nobody understands, a wedding ring that will not crush under a boot heel, a house named after pigeons, a bird with a broken wing over the water: the objects are placed and then left alone.

techniques.name: Music as event
techniques.definition: Performance used to cause something in the plot rather than to decorate a scene.
techniques.inThisBook: Adèle's playing makes agreeable pictures; Mademoiselle Reisz's playing causes physical collapse in a public room, and the difference between the two performances is the difference between the two futures on offer.

techniques.name: Foils
techniques.definition: A character constructed to throw another's choices into relief by making different ones.
techniques.inThisBook: Adèle and Mademoiselle Reisz are the two available lives — the adored mother and the unloved artist — and Chopin makes both of them genuinely attractive and genuinely insufficient, so that Edna is refusing a real choice rather than a straw one.

techniques.name: What is left out
techniques.definition: Decisive events placed in the gaps between chapters rather than on the page.
techniques.inThisBook: The night with Arobin, the removal to the pigeon house, and the final walk into the water are all handled by omission or by a change of scene, which is why the book could be published at all in 1899 and why its ending is still argued about.

quotations.text: looking at his wife as one looks at a valuable piece of personal property which has suffered some damage
quotations.context: Léonce, having told Edna she is burnt beyond recognition, on her return from the beach.
quotations.analysis: The simile is the narrator's, not Léonce's, and it is dropped into an otherwise placid domestic paragraph without comment. Two sentences later Edna is holding out her hands to be given back her rings, which the novel lets the reader connect on their own.

quotations.text: An indescribable oppression, which seemed to generate in some unfamiliar part of her consciousness, filled her whole being with a vague anguish.
quotations.context: Alone on the porch at night, after Léonce has scolded her for neglecting the children and gone to sleep.
quotations.analysis: Every term in the sentence is an admission of ignorance — indescribable, unfamiliar, vague — and the vagueness is precise rather than lazy. Chopin will not let Edna have a word for her own condition at the moment she first feels it, which is what distinguishes this book from a novel of grievance.

quotations.text: In short, Mrs. Pontellier was not a mother-woman.
quotations.context: After an account of how the Grand Isle mothers idolise their children.
quotations.analysis: 'In short' pretends that the sentence is a summary of the preceding paragraph, when in fact it is the introduction of a category that did not exist before Chopin coined it. The hyphen is doing the work: motherhood is being described as a type of person rather than a relationship, which is the first step in separating the two.

quotations.text: A certain light was beginning to dawn dimly within her
quotations.context: At the start of the short chapter that stands back from the story to explain what is happening to Edna.
quotations.analysis: The clause is completed in the corpus by a phrase that takes the promise straight back: the light shows the way and forbids it. Chopin puts her heroine's whole predicament into one image before the plot has moved at all, and the novel spends thirty-three chapters demonstrating that the prohibition was accurate.

quotations.text: In short, Mrs. Pontellier was beginning to realize her position in the universe as a human being, and to recognize her relations as an individual to the world within and about her.
quotations.context: The narrator's summary of the change taking place over the summer.
quotations.analysis: The phrasing is that of a philosophical treatise, and it is applied to a woman on a holiday gallery who has done nothing more remarkable than agree to a swim. Chopin repeats the formula 'In short, Mrs. Pontellier' from two chapters earlier, so that the negative definition is now answered by a positive one.

quotations.text: The voice of the sea is seductive; never ceasing, whispering, clamoring, murmuring, inviting the soul to wander for a spell in abysses of solitude; to lose itself in mazes of inward contemplation.
quotations.context: The end of the short chapter that explains the summer's effect on Edna.
quotations.analysis: The tense is present and general — this is what the sea does, not what it did that evening — which lifts the sentence out of the narrative and lets it be used again. Note that the invitation is to solitude rather than to freedom, and that the novel takes the offer literally in its last chapter.

quotations.text: But the very passions themselves were aroused within her soul, swaying it, lashing it, as the waves daily beat upon her splendid body.
quotations.context: Listening to Mademoiselle Reisz play, in a room of holidaymakers who applaud politely.
quotations.analysis: Edna had expected music to produce pictures — solitude, hope, longing — and gets the emotions themselves with no images attached. The comparison to the surf is the book's first link between the piano and the Gulf, and it makes the effect of art physical in a novel that is about to make the body the whole question.

quotations.text: A feeling of exultation overtook her, as if some power of significant import had been given her to control the working of her body and her soul.
quotations.context: The night she finally swims, after a whole summer of failing to.
quotations.analysis: The achievement is small — she has crossed a few yards of shallow water — and the language is that of investiture, because what she has actually acquired is the experience of directing herself. 'Body and soul' is the formula Chopin will hand back to her at the end of the novel, when she refuses to let anyone else possess either.

quotations.text: She grew daring and reckless, overestimating her strength. She wanted to swim far out, where no woman had swum before.
quotations.context: Minutes into her first successful swim.
quotations.analysis: The narrator supplies the judgement — overestimating — before Edna has come to any harm, so the reader is warned in the same breath as being exhilarated. 'Where no woman had swum before' is exploration language applied to a stretch of Gulf that men crossed every day, and the qualification is the whole point.

quotations.text: I would give up the unessential; I would give my money, I would give my life for my children; but I wouldn’t give myself.
quotations.speaker: Edna Pontellier
quotations.context: Arguing with Adèle Ratignolle on the beach after Robert's departure.
quotations.analysis: She is drawing a distinction her friend cannot follow, and she knows it — the next sentence admits she is only beginning to understand it herself. Putting life in the middle of the list and self at the end inverts the usual scale of sacrifice, and the novel's ending turns on whether that inversion can be sustained.

quotations.text: Once she stopped, and taking off her wedding ring, flung it upon the carpet. When she saw it lying there, she stamped her heel upon it, striving to crush it.
quotations.context: Alone in the house after quarrelling with Léonce about her abandoned reception day.
quotations.analysis: The gesture fails: the boot heel does not mark the ring, and she puts it back on within the paragraph. Chopin gives her heroine one melodramatic act and then shows the object surviving it undamaged, which is a fair summary of what the institution will do to her rebellion.

quotations.text: It was not a condition of life which fitted her, and she could see in it but an appalling and hopeless ennui.
quotations.context: Leaving the Ratignolles' apartment after an evening of perfect domestic harmony.
quotations.analysis: The scene she has just watched is genuinely happy, and the novel does not undercut it: the failure is one of fit rather than of value. Chopin's refusal to make the alternative life contemptible is what stops the book being a tract, and it is also what leaves Edna with nowhere to go.

quotations.text: She began to do as she liked and to feel as she liked.
quotations.context: After deciding that stamping on a ring was childish, and abandoning her Tuesdays at home.
quotations.analysis: One flat sentence, two verbs, no adverb of approval or alarm, and it describes what would have been a scandal in most novels of the period. The second half is the more radical: she stops performing feelings as well as duties, and the household's whole machinery of visits and callers falls over as a result.

quotations.text: The bird that would soar above the level plain of tradition and prejudice must have strong wings. It is a sad spectacle to see the weaklings bruised, exhausted, fluttering back to earth.
quotations.speaker: Mademoiselle Reisz
quotations.context: Reported by Edna to Arobin, after Reisz felt her shoulder blades to see whether her wings were strong.
quotations.analysis: It reaches the reader at second hand, quoted by a woman repeating a warning she has decided to treat as a joke. Chopin then plants the image where it will be needed: the last chapter opens with a bird with a broken wing coming down to the water, and offers no gloss on it at all.

quotations.text: The pigeon house pleased her. It at once assumed the intimate character of a home
quotations.context: Having moved out of her husband's house into a small rented one around the corner.
quotations.analysis: The name is a servant's joke about the size of the place, and Edna adopts it without embarrassment. The passage goes on to describe a sense of having gone down in the social scale and risen in the spiritual one, which is the novel's most explicit statement that independence here is also a reduction.

quotations.text: I am no longer one of Mr. Pontellier’s possessions to dispose of or not. I give myself where I choose.
quotations.speaker: Edna Pontellier
quotations.context: To Robert, who has just explained that he had dreamed of Léonce setting her free.
quotations.analysis: She answers the offer by rejecting its grammar: the question of who may dispose of her does not arise. It is the clearest thing she says in the book, it is addressed to the man she loves, and he is unable to hear it — the next time she is in the room he has gone, leaving a note about loving her enough to leave.

quotations.text: Think of the children, Edna. Oh think of the children! Remember them!
quotations.speaker: Adèle Ratignolle
quotations.context: Whispered, in an exhausted voice, immediately after Adèle's confinement.
quotations.analysis: Three imperatives from a woman who has just given birth, addressed to the one person in the room who did not want to be there. Chopin gives the novel's decisive sentence to the sweetest character in it, and makes it an appeal rather than an argument — which is exactly why Edna cannot dispose of it.

quotations.text: perhaps it is better to wake up after all, even to suffer, rather than to remain a dupe to illusions all one’s life
quotations.speaker: Edna Pontellier
quotations.context: Walking home with Doctor Mandelet from Adèle's bedside.
quotations.analysis: It is the only assessment of her own awakening that Edna offers anybody, and it is hedged twice — 'perhaps', 'after all' — as though she were still working it out on the pavement. The doctor has just described the illusions as a trap set by nature to secure mothers for the race, so her reply is an answer to a theory as well as a statement about herself.

quotations.text: A bird with a broken wing was beating the air above, reeling, fluttering, circling disabled down, down to the water.
quotations.context: On the empty beach at Grand Isle, out of season.
quotations.analysis: Mademoiselle Reisz's warning about weaklings fluttering back to earth arrives as an event in the landscape, twelve chapters later and without a word of commentary. Whether the reader takes it as Edna's verdict on herself or as something merely happening on the beach is left entirely open, and the sentence is placed between two blocks of prose about the sea.

quotations.text: How strange and awful it seemed to stand naked under the sky! how delicious! She felt like some newborn creature, opening its eyes in a familiar world that it had never known.
quotations.context: On the beach, having left her bathing suit on the sand.
quotations.analysis: Two exclamations with opposite charges in the same breath, and then a birth image at the end of a life. 'A familiar world that it had never known' is the whole novel in nine words: nothing around her has changed, and she is seeing it for the first time.

quotations.text: But they need not have thought that they could possess her, body and soul.
quotations.context: Thinking of Léonce and the children while swimming out.
quotations.analysis: The verb is the one from the wedding-ring and property scenes, and the objects are now her husband and her sons together. The sentence is in free indirect style, so the reader cannot tell whether it is a conclusion or a last piece of self-persuasion — which is where Chopin leaves the entire ending.

quotations.text: And you call yourself an artist! What pretensions, Madame! The artist must possess the courageous soul that dares and defies.
quotations.speaker: Mademoiselle Reisz
quotations.context: Imagined by Edna in the water, as the sneer Reisz would have given her.
quotations.analysis: The one standard Edna is still measuring herself against is delivered in a voice she is supplying herself, from a woman who is not present. It is the last piece of dialogue in the novel, and it is a rebuke — the book ends with its heroine inventing her sternest critic and then going on.

quotations.text: There was the hum of bees, and the musky odor of pinks filled the air.
quotations.context: The last sentence of the novel.
quotations.analysis: The book closes on a Kentucky garden from Edna's childhood, in the present tense of memory, with no statement about the water at all. Bees and flowers rather than drowning: Chopin ends on the sensory world that Edna's awakening began in, and refuses to write the sentence a reader is waiting for.

timeline.label: Kate O'Flaherty born in St Louis
timeline.detail: Of Irish and French Creole descent; her father was killed in a railway accident when she was five.

timeline.label: Marriage to Oscar Chopin, and a move to New Orleans
timeline.detail: The twelve years in Louisiana gave her nearly all the material of her fiction.

timeline.label: Oscar Chopin dies
timeline.detail: Chopin ran the family business for a time and then returned to St Louis with six children.

timeline.label: At Fault, her first novel
timeline.detail: Published at her own expense, and little noticed.

timeline.label: The hurricane destroys Chênière Caminada
timeline.detail: The Gulf community Edna visits with Robert had been devastated a few years before the novel was written.

timeline.label: Bayou Folk
timeline.detail: The Louisiana stories that made her reputation as a regional writer, which is the reputation The Awakening broke.

timeline.label: A Night in Acadie, and the novel begun
timeline.detail: A second story collection appeared while she was at work on the book, then titled A Solitary Soul.

timeline.label: The manuscript finished
timeline.detail: Dated 21 January 1898, more than a year before it reached print.

timeline.label: Published by Herbert S. Stone & Company
timeline.detail: On 22 April, in Chicago. Reviewers treated the book as a moral question rather than a literary one.

timeline.label: Removed from Evanston Public Library
timeline.detail: A documented removal. The often-repeated claim that St Louis libraries banned the book has no evidence behind it.

timeline.label: Chopin dies in St Louis
timeline.detail: On 22 August, five years after the novel appeared and with her third story collection still unpublished.

timeline.label: Per Seyersted's biography and collected works
timeline.detail: The scholarly edition and critical study that returned the novel to print and to serious reading.

places.name: Grand Isle, Louisiana
places.note: The barrier-island resort where the novel opens and closes: Creole New Orleans families summering in a row of cottages.

places.name: Chênière Caminada
places.note: The fishing settlement west of Grand Isle that Edna and Robert cross to for mass, destroyed by the hurricane of 1893.

places.name: New Orleans
places.note: The Esplanade Street house, the atelier, the races and the pigeon house around the corner.

places.name: St Louis, Missouri
places.note: Chopin's birthplace, the city she returned to as a widow, and where she wrote the novel.

places.name: Chicago
places.note: Where Herbert S. Stone & Company published the book in April 1899.

criticalViews.position: A novel about a woman's self-ownership
criticalViews.summary: The reading that returned the book to the syllabus after 1969: Edna's refusals — of the reception day, the ring, the household, and finally of being disposed of by anyone — form a coherent argument about who a married woman belongs to.
criticalViews.counter: It has to explain an ending in which the self so carefully claimed is put into the Gulf, and explanations of that ending tend to be more confident than the last chapter is.

criticalViews.summary: Some readers take the last swim as defeat — the weakling fluttering back to earth that Mademoiselle Reisz predicted — and others as the only act left that nobody else can direct. The novel supplies the bird, the sea passage and a childhood garden, and declines to say.
criticalViews.counter: The refusal may itself be the point: Chopin ends in free indirect style, so the last thoughts on the page are Edna's rather than the book's.

criticalViews.summary: Chopin was known as a writer of Louisiana local colour, and the book can be read as the culmination of that work: Creole manners, the Gulf, the Chênière, a society observed from just inside it.
criticalViews.counter: The technique — short chapters, withheld judgement, decisive events left in the gaps — belongs with Flaubert and with the novel of the next twenty years rather than with regional sketch-writing.

criticalViews.summary: More recent criticism has attended to the quadroon nurse, the cook, the servants at Grand Isle and the woman called Old Celestine, and to the fact that Edna's leisure to paint and to think is produced by other women's labour, largely unremarked by the narrator.
criticalViews.counter: The novel does notice the arrangement in places, and its silences are those of the class it describes; the question is how far a reader should credit Chopin with observing what she does not comment on.

essayQuestions.question: How does Chopin present Edna's awakening without endorsing or condemning it?
essayQuestions.focus: Narrative distance and free indirect style
plan: Establish the method with Chapter VI, where the narrator explains Edna's condition in treatise language and then hands the chapter to the sea.
Show how judgements are offered but unattributed — 'overestimating her strength' in Chapter X is the clearest case.
Examine the flatness of 'She began to do as she liked' as a deliberate refusal of emphasis.
Compare the decisive events that happen off the page: the night with Arobin, the move, the last swim.
Conclude on the last two chapters, and what free indirect style does to the reliability of Edna's final thoughts.

essayQuestions.question: 'Adèle and Mademoiselle Reisz are the two futures on offer, and both are insufficient.' Discuss.
plan: Set out the mother-woman passage of Chapter IV and the warmth Chopin allows Adèle throughout.
Set against it the Chapter XVIII evening, where a genuinely happy household produces hopeless ennui in the observer.
Read Mademoiselle Reisz's playing in Chapter IX and her warning in Chapter XXVII as the other offer, with its own costs.
Show how the two women reappear at the end — one whispering about the children, one imagined sneering about pretensions.
Ask what the novel is arguing by refusing to make either life contemptible.

essayQuestions.question: What work does the sea do in The Awakening?
essayQuestions.focus: Repetition, setting and the last chapter
plan: Compare the sea passage as it appears in Chapter VI and again in Chapter XXXIX, noting exactly what changes.
Trace the swim of Chapter X as the novel's first act of self-direction, and its vocabulary of control.
Consider the Gulf as a social space as well as a symbolic one: a resort, a crossing, a fishing village.
Set the bird with the broken wing beside Reisz's warning and ask how the novel wants the connection taken.
Decide what is achieved by ending on a garden in Kentucky rather than on the water.

essayQuestions.question: How far is the novel's subject ownership rather than love?
essayQuestions.focus: Property, money and the pigeon house
plan: Start from Chapter I, where a husband inspects his wife for damage and holds her rings.
Follow the money: the races, the sketches sold, the accounts kept, and the rent on the small house.
Read the wedding-ring scene of Chapter XVII as a failed act against an object that will not be marked.
Use the refusal to Robert in Chapter XXXVI as the novel's most explicit statement.
Weigh the final sentence about being possessed body and soul: whose vocabulary is it, and has it been escaped?

discussionQuestions: Chopin's original title was A Solitary Soul. What changes if you read the book under that title instead?
Adèle is the character the novel is least ironic about, and she says the thing that does the most damage. Why give her that line?
Robert's grand offer is that he might ask Edna's husband to release her. Is he a lover or simply a younger version of Léonce?
The most decisive events in the book happen between chapters. What does Chopin gain by leaving them out?
Edna's freedom to paint depends on servants who are barely described. How should that alter a modern reading?

related.why: Published twenty years earlier and asking the same question from the stage: what a wife owes a house, and what happens when she leaves it.
The other great novel of the 1890s to be reviewed as a moral offence, and another narrator arguing with the judgement his heroine receives.
A later development of the same method: a woman's day, a party, and the whole weight of a life carried in free indirect style.
The nineteenth century's central account of a woman refusing to be disposed of, and the marriage plot Chopin's novel declines to supply.
The American novel of a woman judged publicly for a private life, half a century before Chopin's reviewers reached for the same vocabulary.
